text:
A: Alright? Can you hear me okay? I'm Gary.
B: Hiya Gary, yeah, loud and clear. I'm Daniel. How you doing?
A: Not bad, mate, not bad, cheers. Third one of these now, I'm getting the hang of it. Where are you based then?
B: Peterborough. You?
A: Bridgwater, Somerset. You won't have heard of it unless you've been stuck on the M5.
B: Ha, I have actually, on the way down to Devon with the dog. Lovely sitting in traffic looking at it. So what do you do, Gary?
A: Well, I'm not working at the minute. I was nineteen years at a food distribution depot, forklift, warehouse, a bit of paperwork. Then I did my back in, a prolapsed disc, and the sciatica down my left leg, so I've been signed off just over two year. I still talk about the place like I'm going back Monday, my daughter tells me off for it.
B: Ah, mate, sorry to hear that. Funny enough, I'm in warehousing. I'm operations manager at a distribution centre, homeware and DIY. About a hundred and forty staff across three shifts.
A: Hundred and forty! Blimey. So you're the gaffer.
B: Sort of, yeah, though I spend most of the day walking the floor rather than sat in an office. What were you on, counterbalance?
A: Counterbalance, yeah. I've still got the card in my wallet, lapsed now, mind. I was the one the supervisor sent the new starters to. Show them round, where the toilets are, who to avoid in the canteen. I knew all the agency lads by name.
B: Honestly, that's gold, that. People like you are what keep a shift together. You'd be amazed how much difference one person makes, just someone who says, alright, you're with me today.
A: Well, that's kind of you to say, thank you. I'd love to get back to something, sixteen hours, nothing too heavy. I've been seeing a work coach. Caretaker, car park, meet-and-greet sort of thing.
B: Have you thought about gatehouse or goods-in admin? We've got a lad on our gatehouse, checks drivers in, does the paperwork, sits down most of the time. Chats to everybody. That'd be right up your street.
A: Gatehouse. I never thought of that, you know. I'd be good on a gatehouse, I'm nosy.
B: Ha, that's the main qualification. Worth asking your work coach about, any of the depots round you will have one.
A: I will, I'll write it down after. I write everything down, I've got a calendar on the wall with all my appointments on in biro. Physio Tuesday, food bank Wednesday and Friday.
B: You sound more organised than half my supervisors. I've got colour-coded rotas, my wife thinks it's a medical condition.
A: Ha! Do you get out much, away from work?
B: Parkrun on a Saturday at Ferry Meadows, five-a-side Wednesdays. Started running after my dad had a heart scare a couple of years back, sort of a wake-up call, you know.
A: Yeah. My dad went at sixty-four, a stroke. I'm fifty-six, so I think about it, I won't lie. That's why I do my walks, physio's orders, along the river most days.
B: Good on you, mate. Honestly, that's the main thing, keep moving.
A: Anyway, sorry, I've gone all serious. Do you do a pub quiz? I do Thursdays with three mates, we've never won.
B: Ha, I do the odd one, yeah. What's your team name?
A: "Quiz Team Aguilera". My mate Steve's idea, he thinks it's—
